name: Childersburg Industrial Park
heading: 3. Childersburg Industrial Park — 500 MW proposed
brief: In Talladega County, a proposed $6 billion, 500 MW hyperscale data center would reuse part of the former Alabama Army Ammunition Plant. The mayor described roughly 486 acres in the early agreement, a glycol-based cooling system, and approximately 220 permanent jobs if developed. Inside Climate News documented those figures from the January 2026 city meeting. The site is environmentally sensitive because of its munitions-production history; EPA documents describe the legacy cleanup obligations.

name: Project Marvel, Bessemer
heading: 2. Project Marvel, Bessemer — up to 1,200 MW proposed
brief: Project Marvel near Bessemer is a proposed multi-building campus backed by TPA Group’s Logistic Land Investment and associated with QTS Data Centers. The expanded layout calls for 18 large data-center buildings , substations, retention infrastructure and up to 1.2 GW at full development. The reported capital estimate is approximately $14 billion , but that is not money already spent. A 900-plus-acre rezoning proposal would expand the overall campus toward 1,600 acres. name: Project Red Clay, Lowndes County
heading: 1. Project Red Clay, Lowndes County — up to 1,500 MW requested
brief: Cloverleaf Infrastructure’s Project Red Clay is the largest publicly tracked Alabama proposal by reported power request: 1,500 MW from Alabama Power. The development near Burkville/Hayneville includes plans for four large data buildings and supporting structures. Sources differ on land footprint—early public plans cited roughly 800 acres, while a July stormwater permit identified about 1,044 acres. These numbers describe different planning documents and dates. See the dated project evidence and

name: STaX Franklin Bluffs Bitcoin Mining Pilot
heading: 3. STaX Franklin Bluffs Bitcoin Mining Pilot — 50 MW proposed
brief: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources recorded a May 2025 permit application from STaX Capital Partners for up to 30 acres of pad space roughly 35 miles south of Deadhorse. STaX described multiple 10 MW mobile gas-turbine generators intended to supply 50 MW of modular Bitcoin mining pods in a temporary first-phase proof of concept.

name: DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea Computing Hub
heading: 2. DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea Computing Hub — 100 MW proposed generation
brief: Near Nikiski, DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV has requested a federal preliminary study permit for an underwater compute concept. The September 4 Federal Register notice describes about 330–350 tidal turbines , 66 subsea-compute pods and approximately 3.5 miles of hybrid power/fiber cable to shore. Its estimated 100 MW is potential generation, chiefly intended for the underwater data center—not verified compute load.

name: STAK Energy North Slope Campus
heading: 1. STAK Energy North Slope Campus — 1–3 GW proposed on-site generation
brief: STAK Energy’s proposal is the largest named Alaska computing campus with a disclosed power-design range. The state’s May 12, 2026, preliminary lease notice concerns 715.4 acres about 26 miles south of Deadhorse. Plans involve modular high-performance computing, an on-site gas-fired power plant, associated utilities and 1–3 GW of planned generation at potential full scale.

name: Beale Luckett Road, Marana
heading: 3. Beale Luckett Road, Marana — up to 1,500 MW planned
brief: Beale Infrastructure’s Luckett Road campus spans approximately 600 acres west of Interstate 10 in Marana. The coordinated development comprises two adjacent parcels of roughly 300 acres each. According to the Town of Marana’s official project FAQ , each parcel has an estimated 550–750 MW electrical demand, yielding a 1,100–1,500 MW combined planning range rather than 1.5 GW of installed servers. Tucson Electric Power and Trico Electric Cooperative would serve different parts of the project, and

name: Hassayampa Ranch, West Valley
heading: 2. Hassayampa Ranch, West Valley — up to 1,500 MW proposed
brief: Arizona Land Consulting, led by Anita Verma-Lallian, and investors including Chamath Palihapitiya acquired roughly 2,100 acres for $51 million in 2025 near Tonopah and Buckeye. The developer has discussed a potential 1.5 GW power opportunity and as much as $25 billion in eventual investment if future data-center tenants build out the property. The $25 billion is a potential long-range development value, not verified spending. The developer’s own publication of the Bloomberg report says a utility

name: Tract Buckeye Technology Park
heading: 1. Tract Buckeye Technology Park — up to 1,800 MW planned
brief: Tract’s official Buckeye project page lists 2,019 acres and 1,800 MW of potential capacity for a master-planned technology park west of Phoenix. The developer’s August 2024 acquisition release originally described 2,069 acres, up to 20 million square feet and as many as 40 future data-center buildings, supported by long-term utility planning. The acreage figures reflect differing dated descriptions of the property; neither is a completed-building count.

name: Google West Memphis
heading: 3. Google West Memphis — 270 MW indicative demand estimate; actual campus load undisclosed
brief: Google announced $4 billion of Arkansas investment through 2027 in October 2025, anchored by its first state data center on more than 1,000 acres in West Memphis. Construction is underway. The Arkansas government’s February 2026 water-demand planning presentation estimated approximately 270 MW initial baseload for West Memphis using an assumed watts-per-square-foot ratio. This is a planning estimate, not Google’s announced critical IT load . The same presentation does not specify a verified full

name: Serverfarm Clarksville
heading: 2. Serverfarm Clarksville — 432 MW stated campus design
brief: Serverfarm’s Clarksville ARK campus in Johnson County is among Arkansas’s most advanced projects. Its first 300,000-square-foot building was topped out in October. Data Center Dynamics reported October 12 that the first building is planned for 108 MW , with four buildings totaling 432 MW at full development. An October Arkansas Business investigation describes roughly 430 MW for the first four buildings and a $6.6 billion development supported by up to 40 gas turbines. Later phases could change

name: AVAIO Digital Leo, Pulaski County
heading: 1. AVAIO Digital Leo, Pulaski County — 1,070 MW total baseload design
brief: AVAIO Digital’s current official campus specifications advertise 1,070 MW total baseload power , comprising 570 MW of planned grid supply and 500 MW of behind-the-meter power . The company first announced the project in January with an initial 150 MW Entergy contract and a potential 1 GW expansion. These figures describe supply architecture and buildout plans, not 1,070 MW of operating IT equipment. The current project page describes a 296-acre developed site, while the original announcement dis

name: Google Disk Drive, North San José
heading: 3. Google Disk Drive, North San José — 250 MW disputed computing and research facility
brief: Google has applied to develop up to three research-and-development buildings totaling about 482,790 square feet at 5079–5087 Disk Drive and nearby parcels. The City of San José’s official project notice lists an onsite switching station, substation and associated equipment with 250 MW capacity . Separately, CPUC draft Resolution E-5455 describes a proposed PG&E agreement for a 250 MW Google load at 5079 Disk Drive, with a projected December 2028 service date.

name: Golden Valley Technology Hub, Kern County
heading: 2. Golden Valley Technology Hub, Kern County — 275 MW planned
brief: Beacon Data Centers and California Resources Corporation propose a 275 MW AI-oriented campus at the Elk Hills Oil Field outside Taft. The project would cover about 100 acres , with approximately 400,000 square feet of computing space, an electrical substation and office facilities. The June developer announcement reported by Data Center Dynamics establishes the proposed 275 MW figure; it is not energized capacity.

name: Prologis STEM Park, San José
heading: 1. Prologis STEM Park, San José — 396 MW planned data centers
brief: Prologis STEM Park is the largest documented California proposal in this ranking. The developer’s conceptual plan for approximately 159 acres of city-owned land near Zanker Road and the San José–Santa Clara Regional Wastewater Facility includes four data-center buildings at 99 MW each , or 396 MW total . A separate advanced-manufacturing component is estimated at 100 MW and is not included in the 396 MW data-center ranking. The City of San José’s official project memorandum lists the building-by

name: Westbridge Fontus
heading: 3. Westbridge Fontus — 380+ MW proposed data-center capacity
brief: Westbridge Renewable Energy announced Fontus in July 2025 as a 380+ MW Colorado campus , near major population centers and a carrier-neutral fiber hub. Westbridge says it has secured the land, completed environmental-feasibility assessments and identified available fiber. The company is still pursuing electrical grid and natural-gas interconnections . Its current Fontus project page does not establish a construction start date or fully energized server capacity.

name: Vantage Trident
heading: 2. Vantage Trident — approximately 500 MW total demand, 334 MW IT load
brief: Vantage Data Centers is advancing a contested two-building campus near East 48th Avenue and E-470 in Aurora , next to the Green Valley Ranch area. In a written statement to Capital & Main , Vantage vice president Mark Freeman described 334 MW of computing capacity and approximately 500 MW total electrical demand when computing plus cooling and other facility overhead are counted. The proposal encompasses about 143 acres and more than 860,000 square feet in two two-story buildings; it is not oper

name: Cielo Hudson
heading: 1. Cielo Hudson — 750 MW proposed power capacity
brief: The largest reported Colorado proposal is Cielo Digital Infrastructure’s Hudson campus in Weld County. Rocky Mountain PBS reported in July that the project could cover approximately 500 acres and require 750 MW of power capacity . An Axios September analysis independently listed Hudson as Colorado’s largest planned data-center development. It is still proposed , and a firm construction commencement, fully signed IT-load commitment and energization date are not established in the reviewed sources

name: New Britain Energy & Innovation Park
heading: 3. New Britain Energy & Innovation Park — 44 MW proposed computing phase
brief: At 480 Myrtle Street , the former Stanley Black & Decker complex has already received a substantial piece of energy infrastructure: a 19.98 MW fuel-cell installation . But the associated 44 MW high-performance-computing center was described separately as a future phase in EIP Investment’s Connecticut Siting Council petition . It would reuse older industrial buildings and be followed by additional generation, computing and technology development. The originally discussed $1 billion figure covered

name: O&G Industries Beacon Falls
heading: 2. O&G Industries Beacon Falls — 100 MW marketed capacity
brief: A former quarry near Lopus Road and Route 8 is being offered for a data center that 2026 commercial marketing materials describe as 100 MW and approximately 294,000 square feet . The concept includes on-site natural-gas fuel cells, but neither a named hyperscale tenant nor a firm 100 MW IT-power contract is established. The property was previously the subject of a 32 MW municipal agreement in 2022. That agreement expired in 2023 without a buyer.

name: Global Common Cromwell
heading: 1. Global Common Cromwell — more than 300 MW potential IT power
brief: Global Common is marketing a 159-acre campus around Geer Street in Cromwell with approximately 40 MW of initial IT power and a possible full buildout exceeding 300 MW IT . Unlike the other entries, the developer explicitly identifies the power figure as computing load. The plan would use natural-gas fuel cells supplied through interstate pipeline infrastructure. Global Common says it has a gas supply agreement with Emera Energy and is seeking long-term firm transportation service from Enbridge.

name: Data Canopy Newark
heading: 3. Data Canopy Newark — 6 MW Building Power (Operating)
brief: At 350 Pencader Drive in Newark , Data Canopy’s current operator specification gives the facility 6 MW of building power , supported by three utility feeds. The listing describes 16,085 square feet of white space , 2N and N+1 uninterruptible-power-system arrangements, Generac generators and more than 60 hours of on-site fuel supply. This is a standing enterprise colocation and managed-hosting site, not a newly announced 6 MW buildout.

name: DāSTOR New Castle
heading: 2. DāSTOR New Castle — 8 MW Power (Operating)
brief: At 3 Boulden Circle in New Castle , DāSTOR explicitly specifies 8 MW of power for a 61,000-square-foot building, along with generator-backed power, 2N+1 UPS, 2N networking and N+1 cooling. The company announced its acquisition in April 2024 , citing more than 30,000 square feet of raised floor space. The 61,000-square-foot number is total building footprint, not white-space floor area.

name: Middletown Technology Center
heading: 1. Middletown Technology Center — 50 MW Historical Projected Demand (Not Verified Built)
brief: The largest defensible non-cancelled historical development figure in this narrow documented set belongs to the Middletown Technology Center , proposed by Cirrus Delaware on land within the Middletown Auto Park. The original 2016 air-permit application specifies 50 MW projected demand at completion , with power-generation equipment capable of 62.5 MW . The difference was a 12.5 MW redundant generation allowance —not an additional 12.5 MW of server demand. The filing described approximately 60 ac

name: Atlas Compute
heading: 3. Atlas Compute — Fort Pierce, 240 MW Planned
brief: Atlas Compute publicly describes a 240 MW AI-ready data-center campus in Florida, designed for high-density GPU computing. WFLX’s March 12 reporting ties its proposed site to Midway Industrial Park in the Fort Pierce area of St. Lucie County, where the company had secured land and a zoning-verification letter covered parcels around Post Office Road. The project was publicly discussed as a possible 2027 operation, not a guaranteed energization date. As of that March report, county staff said no f

name: Cielo Digital Infrastructure
heading: 2. Cielo Digital Infrastructure — Haines City, 300 MW Target (Stalled)
brief: The 300 MW Cielo campus was identified near Marion Road and State Road 544 East in Haines City, Polk County. Data Center Dynamics’ July 17 investigation described a project on roughly 74 acres , seeking about 150,000 gallons of water per day . That daily water figure is a proposed demand, not documented actual consumption. Public officials interviewed by FOX 13 said the city lacked sufficient available permitted water capacity and had received no formal development agreement, site plan or zoning

name: Stonebridge / Fort Meade
heading: 1. Stonebridge / Fort Meade — 1,200 MW Proposed Electrical Load (Locally Approved)
brief: The largest substantially documented Florida proposal is Stonebridge’s planned campus on approximately 1,330 acres west of U.S. 98 in Fort Meade . In a June 15 public discussion, a Stonebridge principal described the scheme as 1.2 GW of power; the original recorded discussion is linked by Data Center Record . This is an announced campus electrical-load figure , not 1.2 GW of metered demand or a verified IT-only rating. The city’s commission voted unanimously on April 14 to approve a development
